question: What source-bounded freshwater and brackish-water fish and feeding evidence does Blanco (1956) report for the Laoag River goby-fry fishery?

source.title: Assay of the Goby Fry (Ipon) Fisheries of the Laoag River and Its Adjacent Marine Shores, Ilocos Norte Province
source.author: Guillermo J. Blanco
source.publication: The Philippine Journal of Fisheries, volume 4, issue 1, pp. 31–83 (1956)
source.citation: Blanco, G. J. (1956). Assay of the goby fry (ipon) fisheries of the Laoag River and its adjacent marine shores, Ilocos Norte Province. The Philippine Journal of Fisheries, 4(1), 31–83.
source.archivePublisher: National Fisheries Research and Development Institute (NFRDI), official journal archive
source.reviewedPages: Scanned article pages 31–37: title/abstract, study context, river name list, ipon-run summary, and feeding section.

waterbodyContext: Laoag River, including source-described brackish and freshwater portions
Adjacent marine shores discussed as a separate fishery context
scope.fieldPeriod: The article says three field trips were undertaken from November 1954 to February 1955. It describes six ipon runs spanning September–December 1954 and January–February 1955; exact collection dates for each named point are not given.
scope.localityResolution: The article refers to the Laoag River and various points using these place-name labels, but supplies no coordinates, station boundaries, administrative crosswalk, or per-name taxon/date matrix in the reviewed pages. The labels are preserved as printed and are not independently georeferenced.
scope.samplingContext: The paper covers goby-fry runs, fishery gear, river and watershed conditions, and adjacent marine shores. It distinguishes catches at river points from the broader marine-shore and river-mouth fishery context. The article names paculod and kitang for juvenile gobies at various river points, and chinchorro and tangal nets for fry runs at marine shores and river mouths.
scope.sourceTaxonLabelNote: Names are transcribed from the original article and are not normalized or matched to modern accepted taxa. No specimen or museum-voucher crosswalk is supplied in the reviewed pages.

dietEvidence.sourceFinding: The article describes juvenile gobies at sand-bar margins, river pools, and gravelly bottoms feeding on detritus attached to stones. It says microscopic examination of material taken from young-goby stomachs showed mostly algal and diatom material. It separately describes adult and young paliling (Sicyopterus lacrymosus), bukto (Chonophorus melanocephalus), and bunog (Chonophorus ocellaris) scraping organic matter, mostly diatoms and detritus, from stones in rapid-flowing streams.
dietEvidence.evidenceType: Historical qualitative stomach-material and feeding-behavior observations from the Laoag River study; no quantitative diet table, stomach sample count, or species-by-stomach linkage appears in the reviewed pages.
dietEvidence.interpretationLimit: Keep this attributed to Blanco's 1954–1955 study and its reported juvenile river habitat. It does not support a current diet profile, a universal goby diet, or a modern species-specific dietary claim for the source labels.

assessment.interpretation: This is a valuable historical primary source for the Laoag River goby fishery and for qualitative feeding evidence. Its list is limited to the article's historical source names and broad river-water sections; the study does not provide a machine-readable species-by-site event dataset. Its adjacent marine-shore discussion is not treated as freshwater occurrence evidence.
assessment.reuseFinding: The scanned article is accessible from the official NFRDI journal archive, but no item-specific reuse license or permission for redistribution of derived tables, text, plates, or figures was identified. Only bibliographic metadata and source-attributed research notes are recorded; no article pages, tables, plates, figures, or raw files are included.

disposition.reason: The article supplies useful historical fish and qualitative diet evidence but lacks station coordinates, per-site/taxon/date assignments, specimen crosswalks, a modern taxonomy review, quantitative diet linkage, and item-specific reuse terms. Keep the evidence source-bound and research-only.

nextAction: Preserve Blanco's original names and habitat context. Seek an independently verifiable specimen or modern site-specific survey before making canonical taxon, current-occurrence, or public diet records; check source-specific reuse terms before reusing any article content.
